Chapter 6: Rediscovering Self-Care and Everyday Joy
After years of living on high alert, self-care can honestly feel almost foreign, can’t it? If you’ve spent a long time shaping your days around someone else’s needs or moods, it’s easy to forget what comfort—or even pleasure—looks like just for you.
But now, in the quiet that follows the storm, there’s this gentle, maybe unfamiliar question: What do I actually enjoy? What makes me feel safe, or even a little bit happy?
Picture this: One afternoon, a woman who had survived a controlling relationship found herself wandering through a local park. She noticed the sunlight pouring through the trees, the sound of children laughing, the simple joy of fresh air filling her lungs. For the first time in ages, she felt truly present—right there in her own life. That’s when it hit her: Healing isn’t just about fixing what’s broken. It’s about finding those tiny moments of peace and beauty, even when the day is hard.
Most people don’t realize just how much abuse can dull the senses. It’s like walking through life in survival mode—always watching for danger, rarely stopping to notice anything good. Joy starts to feel out of reach. Relaxing, letting your guard down? That can take time to relearn.
And let’s be honest—self-care isn’t always about bubble baths or spa days. Sometimes, it’s as simple as making your favorite meal, putting on music that stirs up old memories, or heading out for a walk with no destination in mind. For one man, self-care meant shutting off his phone for an hour every evening—giving himself permission to be truly unreachable. For another, it was about reconnecting with a childhood hobby: painting, gardening, playing an instrument—anything that reminded her of who she was before all the pain.
But here’s something a lot of us wrestle with—guilt. If you were raised to put everyone else first, self-care can feel selfish or even indulgent. Yet over time, it becomes clear: Taking care of yourself isn’t a luxury. It’s a necessity. Without it, healing just stalls, and old wounds stick around.
One person described her turning point like this: She bought herself a bouquet of flowers, just because she wanted them. It was such a small gesture, but it felt revolutionary—a quiet way of saying, My happiness matters. And when moments like this are repeated, they start to rebuild a sense of agency and self-worth piece by piece.
Rediscovering joy isn’t about erasing the past or pretending everything’s fine. It’s about making space—for hope, for laughter, for the idea that life can be more than just survival. As self-care becomes a habit, the world starts to open up. New friendships take root, old dreams come back into focus, and the future doesn’t feel quite so daunting.
